items.name: Häagen-Dazs
clues: Rich, indulgent and a little bit grown-up. It sounds expensive before you even taste it.
People treating themselves on the sofa, and anyone who thinks ordinary supermarket tubs are beneath them.
A family that had sold ice cream around the Bronx from a horse-drawn cart since the 1920s started it there around 1960.
Small, expensive tubs of ice cream. It began with just three flavours: vanilla, chocolate and coffee.
The name means nothing in any language. The founder made it up to sound Danish, and the first tubs showed a map of Denmark.
A double name with a hyphen in the middle and an umlaut, even though Danish doesn’t use umlauts.

items.name: Superdry
clues: Relaxed and sporty, with a bit of vintage America and a lot of Japan.
Students, festival-goers and people who like a big logo across the chest.
Started in Cheltenham, England, in 2003, after its founders came back from a trip to Tokyo.
Hoodies, T-shirts and windcheater jackets covered in Japanese writing.
The Japanese on the clothes isn’t supposed to make sense: the company admitted it came from a machine translator. David Beckham was an early fan.
Its English name sounds like a weather forecast for a desert.

items.name: Hollister
clues: Sunny, sporty and laid-back: endless summer, even in a German February.
Teenagers, mostly, and their parents’ bank cards.
Its official story says it was founded in 1922. In fact an American fashion company invented it in 2000.
Hoodies, T-shirts and shorts with a Californian surf look.
Its first shop opened in a shopping centre in Columbus, Ohio, hundreds of kilometres from the nearest ocean.
The little sister of Abercrombie & Fitch, named after an invented founder. There’s also a real town in California with the same name.

items.name: Bacardi
clues: Sunny, sociable and a bit loud. It wants you to think of beaches and dancing, not of the morning after.
Students at house parties, people on holiday and anyone ordering a mojito at happy hour.
A man who had emigrated from Spain bought a small distillery in Santiago de Cuba in 1862.
White rum, the main ingredient in a mojito.
After the Cuban revolution, all its Cuban assets were confiscated in 1960. The family company now has its headquarters in Bermuda, not Cuba.
Its logo is a bat: the founder’s wife saw fruit bats living in the roof of the first distillery. The name is the founder’s surname.

items.name: Nutella
clues: Sweet, family-friendly and comforting. It’s all about breakfast and happiness.
Children, students and anyone eating it straight from the jar with a spoon.
After the Second World War cocoa was scarce and expensive in north-west Italy, so a pastry maker used local hazelnuts instead.
A chocolate-and-hazelnut spread in a glass jar, launched in 1964.
An American blogger started a ‘World Day’ for it in 2007. It’s on 5 February every year.
Made by Ferrero, the company behind Kinder and Rocher. Its name starts with the English word for what’s inside.

items.name: Fanta
clues: Bright, bubbly and silly. Its adverts are loud and colourful, and it never takes itself seriously.
Children at birthday parties, and adults who find cola a bit too serious.
Created in Germany in 1940, during the Second World War, when the German branch of an American drinks company could no longer get the syrup for its famous cola.
A fizzy orange drink in a bright orange bottle, though there are dozens of other flavours around the world.
The first version wasn’t orange at all: it was made from what wartime Germany had, including whey and apple pulp left over from juice-making.
Its name comes from the German word ‘Fantasie’: the boss told his team to use their imagination. Today it belongs to Coca-Cola.
